newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African opposition makes political waves.
newsitem.headline: S.African opposition makes political waves.

text.p: Opposition leaders Roelf Meyer and Bantu Holomisa are making waves in South African politics, but analysts said it was too soon to tell whether their latest gains from existing parties constituted a sea-change.
Meyer, a white Afrikaner, and Holomisa, a black Xhosa from President Nelson Mandela's Transkei homeland, on Thursday won 10 recruits in the Pretoria City Council to their fledgling party.
The 10 said they had quit former president F.W. de Klerk's mainly white National Party (NP) because it remained wedded to the ethnic divisions of apartheid, which ended formally in 1994.
"We believe in political cooperation rather than mere opposition...a new South Africanism rather than those factors that divide us," they said in a statement.

Meyer, expelled recently from the NP, and Holomisa, ousted earlier this year from Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC), plan to launch an as-yet unnamed moderate opposition party on September 27.
Both were charged with undermining their parties by voicing public criticism of their policies or practices.
"This is a body blow, but it's not a knock-out punch," said one NP member. "Meyer's group has a long way to go before it proves it has a future."
Thursday's defection cost the NP control of the council in Pretoria, the Afrikaner capital synonymous with white domination for more than 50 years.
With the Meyer-Holomisa group now holding the balance of power between the NP and the ANC, they will be able for the first time to demonstrate their political potential.

"There are many individuals who have left the National party and the ANC (African National Congress ) to join us, but this was the first big group of people actually holding elected office," Holomisa told Reuters on Friday.
"This could be the beginning of a trend that will be echoed in the other provinces," he said.
Peter Leon, leader of the liberal Democratic Party in Gauteng province, which includes Pretoria and Johannesburg, said defections from de Klerk's "Nats" would destroy the party.
"The Nat bus is on skid row with passengers jumping out before the final crash," he said.
The white-supremacist Conservative Party said the defections should galvanise Afrikaner opposition to Mandela's ANC and convince Afrikaners to stand together for their own survival.

"For the Afrikaner who has already lost political self-determination, the time has arrived to make an unambiguous choice between permanent subjugation in a unified state and freedom for the Afrikaner nation," said spokesman Pieter Aucamp.

Stellenbosch University political analyst Willie Breytenbach said, however, the Meyer-Holomisa group would need considerably more support to be able to stake a claim in South Africa's traditionally rigidly defined political landscape.

"Roelf Meyer's party doesn't have a name and, worse still, it doesn't have policies. This is an initiative by two people with grievances against their former establishment: Meyer against the Nats and Holomisa against the ANC," he said.
Their movement would not become credible until it won significant financial support and it would not attract donors until it demonstrated credibility, he said.
"Modern politics cannot be driven without money," he said.
